text: Kanban supports teams that receive work continuously including support
and maintenance operations It makes flow visible and supports
delivery predictability Picture a support team receiving authentication failures
dashboard requests and small mobile fixes throughout the day
Work arrives continuously so the team needs visibility into
what is active what is waiting and what is
becoming old Kanban helps the team define and improve
that flow A board is part of the approach
but the board alone cannot solve capacity problems The
team also needs explicit policies limits and regular inspection
We will follow five fictional requests and show how
testing contributes to finishing valuable work rather than becoming
an invisible queue near the end
Represent requests as cards moving through Backlog Ready Development
Testing and Done The board exposes current status and
queues Define the workflow before drawing columns Backlog contains
possible work Ready contains requests that meet the team's
entry policy Development contains active implementation Testing contains active
or queued verification and Done meets the agreed completion
policy These are illustrative choices not required Kanban column
names Make the start and finish points explicit because
metrics depend on them A blocked item should remain
visible in the system with its blocker rather than
being moved somewhere that hides its age The board
should represent how work actually flows including waiting that
the team may otherwise overlook
Limit active work to reduce context switching If Testing
has three items and its limit is three finish
or unblock existing work before pulling more Adjust limits
to actual capacity Suppose Testing has a limit of
three items and already contains three Two depend on
an unavailable environment while the third needs a small
fix Starting several more features increases active work without
increasing finished value The team might help restore the
environment and pair on the small fix When an
item finishes capacity becomes available to pull more A
limit is a policy that encourages this discussion it
is not a magic number copied from another team
Review whether the chosen limits support collaboration and manageable
flow then adjust through explicit experiments rather than quietly
ignoring them
Lead time is measured from a defined request or
commitment point to completion cycle time is measured from
the start of work to completion Agree on boundaries
before comparing results Use timestamps to explain flow measures
A request arrives Monday becomes active Wednesday and finishes
Friday If the team measures request-to-finish time that includes
the waiting before Wednesday If its cycle-time boundary starts
when work becomes active the earlier waiting is outside
that measure State whether you use elapsed calendar time
or working time The current Kanban Guide emphasizes work
in progress throughput work item age and cycle time
as flow metrics Lead time is also used in
practice with boundaries that must be defined Unlabelled numbers
from different workflows should not be compared as though
they describe the same thing
A growing Testing queue may indicate environment issues oversized
stories weak upstream tests or capacity constraints Improve overall
flow before assuming headcount is the only solution A
constantly full Testing column is a signal not a
diagnosis The cause could be unstable environments large batches
missing acceptance criteria poor testability or a capacity mismatch
Examine individual items and their waiting time before proposing
a solution If every item waits for the same
shared account creating isolated data may help more than
adding another dashboard If large changes arrive in batches
smaller slices and earlier checks may reduce the queue
The objective is better flow through the whole system
so moving a bottleneck to another column without improving
completion does not establish success
Differentiate critical incidents standard enhancements and fixed-date commitments with
clear policies Too many urgent tickets undermine prioritization Classes
of service make tradeoffs explicit when the team chooses
to use them A production authentication outage may qualify
for expedited handling under an agreed policy A normal
dashboard enhancement follows standard capacity A contractual deadline may
require a fixed-date policy These are complementary practices not
mandatory labels for every Kanban system Too many expedited
items undermine predictability because ordinary work is repeatedly interrupted
Define who can invoke an urgent policy what evidence
is needed and how interrupted work remains visible Priority
should reflect consequences and commitments rather than whoever asks
most loudly
A team supporting a website dashboard and mobile app
receives five requests A production authentication issue receives expedited
attention while other items follow available capacity and testing
checks Walk through the five requests One is an
active production login failure two are routine dashboard improvements
one is a mobile display defect and one is
a reporting change with a future commitment Assess the
login incident first because customers cannot access the service
Apply the agreed urgent policy and make the interruption
visible Keep the other items ordered according to value
risk and capacity After the incident fix verify the
important login journeys and capture a regression check where
useful Then inspect the cause so that the team
learns from the interruption instead of simply celebrating a
fast ticket closure
For your exercise investigate a Testing queue that has
remained full for a week Record each item's age
its blocker and the work needed to finish it
Choose one action that could reduce waiting across several
items such as restoring a shared dependency or preparing
independent test accounts Decide how you will observe whether
the action improves completion Do not assume the busiest-looking
column is the only problem it may reflect issues
upstream A strong Kanban discussion connects visible work explicit
policies and evidence about flow to a practical experiment
that the team can inspect
Work item age is especially useful before work finishes
Suppose three testing items are active one started today
one three days ago and one nine days ago
A completed-item average will not explain the oldest item's
current risk because it has not finished yet Inspect
why it is aging Perhaps it depends on a
supplier response or contains a much larger scope than
the others Make the blocker and next action visible
Historical cycle-time data can help the team discuss expectations
but it should not be treated as a guarantee
for every request Different work types and changed conditions
can alter what a reasonable expectation looks like
Avoid maximizing individual utilization at the expense of flow
If developers begin more features whenever testing waits the
board may show impressive activity while customers receive few
completed changes Helping finish an older item can be
more valuable than starting another That might mean clarifying
a rule reducing a change's scope improving testability or
investigating a failing integration together Measure whether completed throughput
and waiting improve under the experiment A work in
progress limit should encourage this system-level conversation It should
not become a rigid excuse to leave a colleague
blocked while everyone else starts work that will soon
join the same queue
Kanban improves transparency and flow Knowledge check what should
be investigated when the Testing column is consistently full
